# Abstract {.unnumbered}

Grant funding decisions are often based on only a small number of expert
reviews, making the uncertainty of proposal rankings difficult to assess. This
report studies the 2026 CRS Seed Grant evaluation, in which 42 proposals each
received two reviews from a panel of nine reviewers. Bayesian hierarchical
modelling is used to separate proposal effects, reviewer-associated scoring
tendencies and residual review-level variation, and to quantify uncertainty in
the resulting ranking.

The main model placed the same four proposals in the first four posterior-mean
positions as the four proposals that qualified under the final CRS decision
rule. However, substantial uncertainty remained about the exact ordering of
individual proposals. The main conclusions were computationally stable and
robust to the tested prior specification, while the continuous Gaussian
treatment of the five-point scores remained an explicit modelling limitation.

Changing the evaluation outcome from the holistic overall grade to an
equal-weight average of the four supporting criteria produced a noticeably
different proposal ordering. Finally, the reviewer--proposal assignment
structure was used to study additional reviews. For small review budgets,
random, disagreement-targeted and sequential A-optimal allocation produced
almost identical reductions in global uncertainty in pairwise proposal
comparisons.

Overall, Bayesian ranking complements transparent decision rules by making
ranking uncertainty explicit and by clarifying when additional review effort is
likely to be informative.


# Introduction

## Grant evaluation under limited information

Grant peer review converts a limited number of expert judgments into decisions
that can have substantial consequences for applicants. The challenge is not
only disagreement between reviewers, but also the risk of overinterpreting
small score differences when each proposal is assessed by only a few reviewers
and when reviewers may differ systematically in how they use the scoring
scale. Kaplan et al. [-@kaplan2008] show directly that finer scoring precision requires
increasingly many independent reviewers, and illustrate how rankings can vary
strongly when only a small number of evaluations are available.

This uncertainty becomes particularly important when proposals are close in
score or close to a decision boundary, such as a funding line. Empirical studies
of grant review have reported instability in funding decisions and low
single-rater reliability, and cross-classified models have been used to separate
proposal- and assessor-related variation [@graves2011; @jayasinghe2003].
Heyard et al. [-@heyard2022] similarly motivate Bayesian ranking by low
inter-rater reliability and the difficulty of distinguishing proposals of
similar quality near a funding line. These findings do not imply that peer review is
uninformative; rather, they motivate distinguishing an observed numerical
ordering from the strength of evidence supporting that ordering.

## CRS Seed Grant evaluation 2026

The Center for Reproducible Science and Research Synthesis (CRS) at the
University of Zurich (UZH) works on reproducibility, research synthesis and
meta-research [@crs2026call]. In 2026, the CRS launched its first Seed Grant
call to support early-stage projects and initiatives in these areas. The
evaluation included 42 proposals assessed by nine reviewers. Each proposal
received exactly two reviews, resulting in 84 completed reviews.

Reviewers evaluated each proposal on four supporting criteria: scientific
quality; potential for scaling and obtaining substantial third-party funding;
relevance to fostering a sustainable, innovative, and diverse Swiss “research
on research” community; and commitment to good research practices, open
science, and reproducibility. Both the four criterion scores and the separate
holistic overall grade were recorded on an integer scale from 1 to 5, with
higher values indicating a more favourable evaluation. Reviewers were not
given a fixed weighting rule for translating the four criterion scores into the
holistic grade; the overall judgment was assigned separately.

The original call described selection using the average score across the four
criteria and reviewers [@crs2026call]. During the development of the evaluation
procedure, this was subsequently replaced by the holistic overall grade, which
became the score used for qualification. The reason for this change was not
documented in the material available for this project.

The call indicated that approximately six projects could be funded [@crs2026call]. In the final evaluation procedure, four proposals met the qualification rule and were selected for funding, as documented on the published results page [@crs2026results]. The rule is reconstructed explicitly in Section 2.2.

## Motivation for Bayesian ranking

The final CRS qualification procedure was transparent and easy to apply, but it
did not quantify how strongly the available reviews separated proposals.
Observed grades may also reflect systematic differences in reviewer scoring
behaviour in addition to proposal-level differences.

Bayesian hierarchical modelling provides a way to represent these sources of
variation separately. Following Heyard et al. [-@heyard2022], proposals can be
ranked using the posterior distribution of latent proposal effects rather than
raw score averages alone, thereby retaining uncertainty about their relative
ordering. In the CRS analysis, Bayesian ranking is therefore used as
uncertainty-aware decision support rather than as a replacement rule that
mechanically determines funding.

## Research questions

### Research Question 1

What ranking does the Bayesian model produce after accounting for reviewer differences, and how uncertain are the resulting ranks?

### Research Question 2

How does the main Bayesian ranking model compare with the final CRS qualification rule and the ranking based on the observed overall grades?

### Research Question 3

Is the main Bayesian model computationally stable, adequate under posterior
predictive checks, and robust to the tested prior specification?

### Research Question 4

How closely do the four supporting criterion scores correspond to the holistic overall grade, and would an equal-weight average of the criteria have produced a materially different proposal ordering?

### Research Question 5

Which single additional reviewer–proposal assignment would most reduce uncertainty under the fitted Bayesian model, and how does this depend on the chosen notion of uncertainty?

## Scope and structure of the report

The holistic overall grade is the main outcome for the Bayesian analysis. The
four supporting criteria are examined separately, including an equal-weight
criterion average used as a descriptive sensitivity analysis rather than as a
preferred scoring rule. V0 reproduces the continuous reference specification of
Heyard et al. [-@heyard2022], while the simpler cross-classified V1 model serves
as the main CRS model. Chapters 4 and 5 present the ranking results and assess
the computational stability, posterior predictive behaviour and prior
sensitivity of V1.

Chapter 6 treats the reviewer--proposal assignment structure as a statistical
design problem. It evaluates hypothetical additional reviews using established
optimal-design criteria and then compares random, disagreement-targeted and
sequential A-optimal allocation for small review budgets. Because reviewer
expertise, conflicts and eligibility are unavailable, these results are
interpreted as statistical design comparisons rather than operational
assignment recommendations. Chapter 7 discusses the findings and their
implications for future CRS evaluations.

# Evaluation design and descriptive analysis

## Evaluation process and analytical data

The pseudonymised analytical dataset contains 84 reviews of 42 proposals by
nine reviewers. Each proposal received exactly two reviews, while reviewers
completed between 6 and 12 reviews. Assignments were based on expertise and
availability.

Each review contains four supporting criterion scores and a separate holistic
overall grade, all recorded as integers from 1 to 5, with higher values
indicating a more favourable evaluation. No fixed weighting formula determined
how the supporting criteria contributed to the separately assigned holistic
grade. The Bayesian models use the holistic overall grade as their outcome; the
criterion scores are retained for a separate descriptive analysis of their
relationship with that grade.

## Reconstruction of the final qualification procedure

According to the published CRS Seed Grant results [@crs2026results], funding was available for proposals that received the highest overall grade from at least one reviewer and no grade below the second-highest category. Since the overall grade was scored on a scale from 1 to 5, this means that a proposal qualified if it received at least one grade of 5 and its second grade was at least 4. With exactly two reviews per proposal, the qualifying score combinations were therefore (5, 5), (5, 4), and (4, 5). Equivalently, a proposal qualified if its mean overall grade was at least 4.5.

This procedure should be interpreted as a score-based qualification threshold rather than as a fixed top-four selection rule. Four proposals satisfied the threshold in the 2026 evaluation round. Since the call indicated that approximately six projects could be funded, the available funding capacity was not binding and no additional prioritization among qualified proposals was required.



## Criteria and holistic overall grade {#sec-criteria-overall}

Previous NIH analyses have shown that individual criterion scores can differ
substantially in their association with holistic overall evaluations
[@eblen2016; @erosheva2020]. This motivates examining whether the four
supporting CRS criteria correspond equally closely to the separately assigned
holistic overall grade.

Let $C_{rc}$ denote the score assigned in review $r$ to criterion $c$, and let
$Y_r$ denote the holistic overall grade. Their relationship was summarized
descriptively using Pearson correlation for linear association and Spearman
correlation for monotonic rank association. The sample definitions are given in
@sec-app-correlation. These correlations are interpreted descriptively because
the 84 reviews are not independent with respect to proposals and reviewers.

| Criterion | Mean criterion score | Pearson correlation with overall grade | Spearman correlation with overall grade |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Scientific quality | 3.643 | 0.892 | 0.890 |
| Community building | 3.179 | 0.545 | 0.551 |
| Scaling potential | 3.512 | 0.541 | 0.553 |
| Scientific rigor | 3.881 | 0.588 | 0.599 |

: Review-level criterion means and their descriptive correlations with the holistic overall grade. {#tbl-criterion-correlations}

Scientific quality showed the strongest relationship with the holistic overall
grade, with Pearson and Spearman correlations of 0.892 and 0.890. The remaining
three criteria were positively related to the overall grade but less strongly,
with correlations around 0.54--0.60. These correlations do not, however,
identify the weights reviewers placed on the individual criteria.

For a simple equal-weight summary, define the criterion average for review $r$ as

$$
A_r
=
\frac{1}{4}\sum_{c=1}^{4}C_{rc}.
$$

Across the 84 reviews, the mean holistic overall grade was 3.476 and the mean
equal-weight criterion average was 3.554. The Pearson correlation between
$A_r$ and $Y_r$ was 0.859 and the Spearman correlation was 0.849. The mean
difference $A_r-Y_r$ was 0.077 grade points, indicating little systematic
difference in level between the two summaries, and 78.6% of reviews had a
criterion average within 0.5 grade points of the holistic overall grade.

## Equal-weight criterion summary at proposal level {#sec-criterion-proposal}

The equal-weight summary is used as a descriptive counterfactual rather than as an estimate of how reviewers actually combined the four criteria. For proposal $i$, let

$$
O_i
=
\frac{1}{2}\sum_{r:p(r)=i}Y_r
$$

denote its mean holistic overall grade, and let

$$
A_i
=
\frac{1}{2}\sum_{r:p(r)=i}A_r
=
\frac{1}{8}\sum_{r:p(r)=i}\sum_{c=1}^{4}C_{rc}
$$

denote the equal-weight average of all eight criterion scores received across its two reviews.

The two proposal-level summaries remained strongly related, with Pearson correlation 0.848 and Spearman correlation 0.881. Their relationship is shown in @fig-proposal-criterion-overall.

![Proposal-level equal-weight criterion average versus mean holistic overall grade. The dashed identity line represents identical proposal-level summaries. CRS qualifiers and proposals with the largest **raw-rank changes** are labelled.](figures/criteria_descriptive/proposal_level_criterion_average_vs_overall.png){#fig-proposal-criterion-overall width=85% fig-pos="H"}

The holistic proposal average is relatively coarse because it is calculated from only two integer-valued grades, whereas $A_i$ averages eight criterion scores and therefore has finer numerical resolution. Raw-rank changes are consequently sensitive to the breaking of ties and are not emphasized here.

At the top of the distribution, P022 had a criterion average of 4.75, while
P032 and P041 had 4.50. These are three of the four proposals that qualified
under the final CRS rule. The fourth qualifier, P023, had a criterion average
of 4.00, while several non-qualified proposals had averages of 4.375. Equal
weighting therefore preserves substantial agreement with the holistic
evaluation but does not reproduce its upper ordering exactly.

# Bayesian ranking framework

## Related work

The Bayesian ranking framework used in this project follows Heyard et al.
[-@heyard2022], who developed a hierarchical model for research-proposal
evaluation at the Swiss National Science Foundation. Each proposal $i$ is
represented by a latent proposal effect $\theta_i$, and uncertainty in the
relative ordering of proposals is retained through the posterior distribution
of these effects.

Their approach builds on earlier Bayesian methods for ranking random effects.
In particular, Laird and Louis [-@laird1989] developed Bayes and empirical-Bayes
methods for estimating ranks in variance-component models. Heyard et al.
summarize posterior ranking uncertainty using the expected rank of each
proposal, which is also the principal Bayesian ranking quantity used in this
report and is defined formally in @sec-posterior-ranking.

Bayesian hierarchical models have also been applied directly to grant-review
ratings. Johnson [-@johnson2008] modelled reviewer scoring differences and
posterior uncertainty in NIH proposal ratings, while Cao, Stokes and Zhang
[-@cao2010] developed an ordinal multirater model for ranking grant proposals.
The proposal--reviewer structure is closely related to the cross-classified
grant-review model of Jayasinghe, Marsh and Bond [-@jayasinghe2003], in which
proposal and reviewer effects are crossed rather than nested.

More recently, Heyard et al. [-@heyard2025] applied Bayesian expected ranks to
individual evaluations of Marie Skłodowska-Curie Actions proposals and compared
them with rankings and funding decisions obtained after consensus meetings.

The present analysis therefore does not introduce a new Bayesian ranking
method. It takes Heyard et al. as its methodological starting point, reproduces
their continuous reference specification as V0, and examines whether a simpler
crossed proposal--reviewer model preserves the substantive ranking conclusions
in the CRS setting.

## V0: Heyard reference model

The reference model V0 reproduces the continuous homogeneous-variance
specification of Heyard et al. [-@heyard2022]. Let $r=1,\ldots,84$ index
completed reviews, let $p(r)$ denote the proposal evaluated in review $r$, and
let $a(r)$ denote the reviewer who produced that review. The observed holistic
overall grade is $Y_r$, $\bar Y$ denotes its sample mean over all 84 reviews,
and $Y=(Y_1,\ldots,Y_{84})^\top$ denotes the full vector of observed grades.

The model is

$$
Y_r \mid \theta,\lambda
\sim
\mathcal{N}\!\left(
\bar Y+\theta_{p(r)}+\lambda_{p(r),a(r)},
\sigma^2
\right),
$$

with

$$
\theta_i\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\tau_\theta^2),
$$

and

$$
\lambda_{ij}\sim\mathcal{N}(\nu_j,\tau_\lambda^2),
\qquad
\nu_j\sim\mathcal{N}(0,0.5^2).
$$

The latent proposal effect $\theta_i$ is the quantity used for ranking.
For reviewer $j$, $\nu_j$ represents a persistent reviewer-specific scoring
tendency. The assessment effect $\lambda_{ij}$ is centred on $\nu_j$, so that
$\lambda_{ij}-\nu_j$ represents an additional deviation specific to reviewer
$j$ evaluating proposal $i$.

V0 is retained as the methodological reference model rather than as the
preferred CRS specification. Each reviewer--proposal pair is observed only once
in the CRS data, so the pair-specific deviation $\lambda_{ij}-\nu_j$ is informed
by only one score and is difficult to distinguish from residual review-level
variation. This motivates the simpler V1 model, which retains persistent
proposal and reviewer effects but removes the additional pair-specific layer.

## V1: CRS cross-classified model

The CRS-specific V1 model simplifies V0 by removing the
proposal--reviewer-specific assessment layer and serves as the main model for
the CRS analysis. Using the indexing defined above,

$$
Y_r
=
\bar Y
+
\theta_{p(r)}
+
b_{a(r)}
+
\varepsilon_r,
\qquad
\varepsilon_r\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^2),
$$

or equivalently,

$$
Y_r
\sim
\mathcal{N}\!\left(
\bar Y+\theta_{p(r)}+b_{a(r)},
\sigma^2
\right).
$$

Here, $\theta_i$ represents the proposal-specific deviation from the overall
mean, $b_j$ represents a persistent reviewer-specific scoring tendency, and
$\varepsilon_r$ captures residual review-level variation. The hierarchical
distributions are

$$
\theta_i\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\tau_\theta^2),
\qquad
b_j\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\tau_b^2).
$$

The proposal effects $\theta_i$ are the quantities used for ranking. Because
reviewer assignments were based on expertise and availability rather than
random allocation, the reviewer effects $b_j$ are interpreted descriptively as
reviewer-associated scoring tendencies rather than as causal measures of
reviewer bias.

V1 is cross-classified because each grade belongs simultaneously to a proposal
and a reviewer, with neither grouping nested within the other. Its hierarchical
structure induces partial pooling: proposal effects are shrunk toward zero,
which corresponds to the overall mean $\bar Y$ on the observed grade scale,
while reviewer effects are pooled analogously. The amount of pooling is
determined by the estimated between-proposal and between-reviewer variation,
$\tau_\theta^2$ and $\tau_b^2$. This regularisation is particularly relevant
because each CRS proposal contributes only two grades.

The likelihood and hierarchical priors are combined through Bayesian updating
to obtain the joint posterior distribution of the model parameters. A detailed
derivation of this updating and the resulting partial pooling is given in
@sec-app-bayesian-updating.

## Assumptions and prior specification

Both V0 and V1 treat the observed grades as conditionally Gaussian with a
common residual variance and assume exchangeable proposal effects around zero.
V1 additionally assumes exchangeable reviewer effects around zero. The overall
mean $\bar Y$ is fixed at the observed sample mean rather than estimated as a
separate intercept.

For V0,

$$
\sigma,\tau_\theta,\tau_\lambda
\sim
\operatorname{Uniform}(0,2),
$$

while V1 uses

$$
\sigma,\tau_\theta,\tau_b
\sim
\operatorname{Uniform}(0,2).
$$

The lower endpoint is implemented numerically as $10^{-6}$. Sensitivity of the
main V1 conclusions to the scale priors is examined in Chapter 5.

Although the holistic overall grade is recorded as an integer from 1 to 5,
both models retain the continuous Gaussian treatment used in the reference
analysis of Heyard et al. [-@heyard2022]. This assumes that adjacent score
categories are equally spaced. Because the primary target is the relative
ordering of latent proposal effects rather than prediction of valid score
categories, this approximation is retained here; its limitations are assessed
through posterior predictive checks in Chapter 5.

## Posterior ranking quantities {#sec-posterior-ranking}

Ranking is based on the posterior distribution of the proposal effects
$\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_{42}$ rather than directly on observed score averages.
For posterior draw $s$, define the rank of proposal $i$ as

$$
R_i^{(s)}
=
1+\sum_{k\neq i}
\mathbb{1}_{\{\theta_k^{(s)}>\theta_i^{(s)}\}},
$$

where rank 1 corresponds to the largest proposal effect and
$\mathbb{1}_{\{\cdot\}}$ denotes the indicator function.

The posterior mean of this rank distribution is the expected rank,

$$
ER_i
=
\operatorname{E}[R_i\mid Y].
$$

Equivalently,

$$
ER_i
=
1+\sum_{k\neq i}
\mathbb{P}(\theta_k>\theta_i\mid Y),
$$

so expected rank is 1 plus the sum of the posterior probabilities that each
competing proposal has a larger latent effect than proposal $i$. It is estimated
from $S$ posterior draws by

$$
ER_i
\approx
\frac{1}{S}\sum_{s=1}^{S}R_i^{(s)}.
$$

Expected rank is the principal Bayesian ranking quantity used in this report
and follows Heyard et al. [-@heyard2022]. With 42 proposals, the midpoint of
the rank scale is 21.5. When pairwise ordering probabilities are close to 0.5,
expected ranks therefore move toward the centre of the rank scale.

Three ranking summaries are distinguished throughout the analysis. The
**raw-score rank** orders proposals by their mean observed overall grade, the
**posterior-mean rank** orders the posterior means of $\theta_i$, and the
**expected rank** averages the rank of proposal $i$ across the posterior
distribution. Rank uncertainty is summarized by the 90% posterior rank
interval, defined by the 5th and 95th percentiles of $R_i$.

For particular proposals, pairwise posterior probabilities such as

$$
\mathbb{P}(\theta_i>\theta_k\mid Y)
$$

provide a direct measure of the evidence that one proposal ranks above another.
They are particularly useful when proposals are nearly tied and small model
changes alter their integer ranks.

## Posterior computation and diagnostics {#sec-posterior-computation}

All Bayesian models were fitted in JAGS from R. V0 used the Heyard reference
specification implemented through `ERforResearch`, while V1 used a custom JAGS
model with one persistent effect per reviewer.

Unless stated otherwise, each final fit used four Markov chains, 10,000
adaptation iterations, 10,000 burn-in iterations and 50,000 retained iterations
per chain, giving 200,000 posterior draws in total. All MCMC fits used the fixed
random seed 20260727 for reproducibility.

Posterior-mean ranks, expected ranks, rank intervals and pairwise posterior
probabilities were calculated from the retained draws. Computational convergence
was assessed using the potential scale reduction factor (PSRF) and effective
sample size (ESS). Statistical model adequacy is assessed separately through
posterior predictive checks and prior sensitivity in Chapter 5.

# Bayesian ranking results

## Main V1 ranking and comparison with the final CRS procedure

Under V1, P022, P032, P023 and P041 occupied posterior-mean ranks 1 to 4,
with expected ranks 13.08, 15.87, 15.87 and 16.22, respectively. These are
exactly the four proposals that satisfied the final CRS qualification threshold.

Because each observed proposal mean is based on only two integer-valued grades,
the observed-score ranking is coarse. The 42 proposals take only seven distinct
mean-score values, so several proposals share the same observed rank before any
model-based adjustment is applied.

Despite the clear posterior-mean ordering, uncertainty in the exact latent ranks
remains substantial. The 90% posterior rank interval for P022 was 1--36; for
P023 and P032 it was 1--37; and for P041 it was 1--38. The observed-score
rank, posterior-mean rank and expected rank are compared in
@fig-v1-ranking-comparison.

The Bayesian analysis therefore does not change the group of four proposals
identified by the CRS procedure, but adds information about how uncertain their
relative latent positions remain. The CRS rule determines qualification from the
observed grades, whereas V1 quantifies uncertainty in the underlying proposal
ordering. It is therefore interpreted as uncertainty-aware decision support
rather than as a retrospective replacement for the qualification rule.

![Proposal rankings under the observed-score ranking, posterior-mean ranking and
posterior expected rank for the V1 cross-classified model. The movement of
expected ranks toward the centre of the rank scale reflects substantial
posterior uncertainty in the exact proposal
ordering.](figures/model_comparison/ranking_comparison_V1.png){#fig-v1-ranking-comparison width=95% fig-pos="H"}

## Robustness of the ranking to the Heyard reference specification

The V0 Heyard reference model produced almost the same ranking as V1. The four
CRS qualifiers again occupied the first four posterior-mean positions. Across
all 42 proposals, the Spearman correlation between posterior-mean ranks was
0.9951 and the Pearson correlation between expected ranks was 0.9916. The
agreement is shown in @fig-expected-rank-v0-v1.

![Posterior expected ranks under the V0 Heyard reference model and the V1
cross-classified model. The dashed identity line represents identical expected
ranks under both models.](figures/model_comparison/expected_rank_v0_vs_v1.png){#fig-expected-rank-v0-v1 width=85% fig-pos="H"}

Small changes in integer ranks nevertheless occurred for proposals that were
almost indistinguishable. Twenty-six of the 42 proposals changed
posterior-mean rank between V0 and V1, but the mean absolute change was only
0.86 positions and the maximum was three. For example, V0 places P023 above
P032, while V1 reverses them. Yet

$$
\mathbb{P}(\theta_{032}>\theta_{023}\mid Y)=0.498955
$$

under V0 and

$$
\mathbb{P}(\theta_{032}>\theta_{023}\mid Y)=0.500470
$$

under V1. The apparent reversal therefore reflects an almost exact posterior
tie rather than meaningful disagreement between the models.

Rank uncertainty was similarly stable. The mean width of the 90% posterior
rank intervals was 36.50 positions under V0 and 36.74 under V1, with median
width 37 under both models. Thus, simplifying V0 to V1 changes little about
either the broad ordering or the conclusion that exact ranks are poorly
identified. Detailed V0 results and computational diagnostics are provided in
@sec-app-v0.

## Bayesian ranking using the equal-weight criterion average

The descriptive analyses in @sec-criteria-overall and @sec-criterion-proposal
show that the holistic grade and equal-weight criterion average contain
overlapping but not identical information. To examine whether this difference
persists after accounting for reviewer-associated scoring tendencies and ranking
uncertainty, V1 was fitted again using the review-level criterion average $A_r$
as the outcome:

$$
A_r
\sim
\mathcal{N}\!\left(
\bar{A}
+
\theta^{(A)}_{p(r)}
+
b^{(A)}_{a(r)},
\sigma_A^2
\right),
$$

with

$$
\theta_i^{(A)}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\tau_{\theta,A}^2),
\qquad
b_j^{(A)}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\tau_{b,A}^2),
$$
where $\bar A$ denotes the observed mean of the 84 review-level criterion
averages.

The reviewer--proposal assignments, priors and MCMC settings were identical to
the overall-grade V1 fit; only the outcome and its observed mean changed. The
fit showed satisfactory computational diagnostics (maximum PSRF 1.0032;
minimum ESS 1,863).

Changing the evaluation outcome had a noticeably larger effect on the ranking
than changing from V0 to V1. The Spearman correlation between posterior-mean
ranks from the two V1 fits was 0.873, while the Pearson correlation between
expected ranks was 0.863. The mean absolute expected-rank change was 2.97
positions and the maximum was 7.89. By comparison, the correlation between V0
and V1 expected ranks for the same holistic outcome was 0.9916. The comparison
is shown in @fig-er-overall-criterion.

![Posterior expected ranks from V1 fitted to the holistic overall grade and to
the equal-weight criterion average. The dashed identity line represents
identical expected ranks under both outcome definitions. CRS qualifiers and
proposals with the largest expected-rank changes are
labelled.](figures/criterion_model_comparison/expected_rank_overall_vs_criterion_average.png){#fig-er-overall-criterion width=82% fig-pos="H"}

The upper ordering also changed. P022 and P032 remained at posterior-mean
ranks 1 and 2, P041 moved from rank 4 to rank 3, and P040 moved from rank 6
to rank 4. P023 showed the largest change among these proposals, moving from
posterior-mean rank 3 to rank 11. That change appears less substantial when
posterior uncertainty is considered: P023's expected rank changed only from
15.87 to 16.80, whereas P040 improved from 18.43 to 12.19. This illustrates
why changes in exact integer ranks should be interpreted together with the
posterior rank uncertainty.

The criterion-average fit produced somewhat narrower posterior rank
distributions: the mean width of the 90% posterior rank intervals decreased
from 36.74 to 33.19 positions and the median from 37 to 34. The criterion
average also had lower observed dispersion than the holistic grade (standard
deviations 0.772 and 0.950, respectively). Because the criterion average itself
combines four scores, part of this reduction in variation may arise mechanically
from averaging. The corresponding variance decomposition is examined in
@sec-variance-diagnostics.

These results do not establish that either outcome is preferable. They show
that the definition of the evaluation outcome has a larger effect on the
posterior ordering than the change from V0 to V1 while holding the holistic
outcome fixed.

# Validation and sensitivity analysis of V1

## Validation strategy

Unless stated otherwise, this chapter evaluates V1 fitted to the holistic
overall grade, the main working model. The close agreement between V0 and V1
shows that the ranking is not sensitive to the additional assessment-specific
layer in V0, but does not establish that V1 adequately represents the observed
reviews.

Validation therefore addresses three questions: whether posterior computation
is stable, whether V1 reproduces important features of the observed grades, and
whether the main conclusions depend materially on the baseline scale priors.

## Computational and variance diagnostics {#sec-variance-diagnostics}

The V1 posterior was sampled reliably. Across all monitored parameters, the
maximum PSRF was 1.0017 and the minimum effective sample size was 1,627. The
corresponding trace plots are provided in @sec-app-trace.

Under V1, the marginal variance of an individual grade is

$$
\operatorname{Var}(Y_r)
=
\tau_\theta^2+\tau_b^2+\sigma^2.
$$

For posterior draw $s$, let the total marginal variance be

$$
V_{\mathrm{tot}}^{(s)}
=
\left(\tau_\theta^{(s)}\right)^2
+
\left(\tau_b^{(s)}\right)^2
+
\left(\sigma^{(s)}\right)^2.
$$

The corresponding variance shares are

$$
\rho_{\mathrm{proposal}}^{(s)}
=
\frac{\left(\tau_\theta^{(s)}\right)^2}{V_{\mathrm{tot}}^{(s)}},
\qquad
\rho_{\mathrm{reviewer}}^{(s)}
=
\frac{\left(\tau_b^{(s)}\right)^2}{V_{\mathrm{tot}}^{(s)}},
\qquad
\rho_{\mathrm{residual}}^{(s)}
=
\frac{\left(\sigma^{(s)}\right)^2}{V_{\mathrm{tot}}^{(s)}}.
$$

For the overall-grade model, their posterior medians were 0.050, 0.026 and
0.896, with corresponding 95% credible intervals of approximately
$[0.0002,0.289]$, $[0.0001,0.240]$ and $[0.615,0.995]$.

![Posterior variance shares under V1. Points show posterior medians and vertical
intervals show 95% credible intervals.](figures/validation/v1_variance_shares.png){#fig-v1-variance-shares width=72% fig-pos="H"}

The proposal variance share also has a reliability interpretation. For two
ratings of the same proposal by different reviewers $j$ and $k$, both ratings
share the same proposal effect $\theta_i$. Under the model's independence
assumptions, this gives

$$
\operatorname{Cov}(Y_{ij},Y_{ik})
=
\tau_\theta^2,
$$

while each rating has marginal variance
$\tau_\theta^2+\tau_b^2+\sigma^2$. Therefore,

$$
\operatorname{Cor}(Y_{ij},Y_{ik})
=
\frac{\tau_\theta^2}
{\tau_\theta^2+\tau_b^2+\sigma^2}
=
\rho_{\mathrm{proposal}}.
$$

Thus, under V1, the proposal variance share is also the model-implied
correlation between two ratings of the same proposal by different reviewers,
corresponding to the cross-classified reliability interpretation of Jayasinghe
et al. [-@jayasinghe2003]. Its posterior median of approximately 0.05 indicates
weak agreement attributable to a shared proposal effect. Most fitted variation
is instead associated with residual review-level variation, helping to explain
the broad posterior ranks despite two ratings per proposal. This decomposition
alone does not, however, establish that the sparse assignment design causes the
ranking uncertainty.

For comparison, the same decomposition was calculated for V1 fitted to the
equal-weight criterion average.

| Response | Proposal share | Reviewer share | Residual share |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Holistic overall grade | 0.050 | 0.026 | 0.896 |
| Equal-weight criterion average | 0.192 | 0.046 | 0.733 |

: Posterior median variance shares under V1 for the holistic overall grade and equal-weight criterion-average outcomes. {#tbl-variance-shares}

The shares sum to one within each posterior draw. Because the table reports
the median of each share separately, the displayed medians need not sum exactly
to one.

The criterion-average fit attributes a larger share of variation to proposals
and a smaller share to residual variation. However, the two decompositions
refer to different outcomes: $A_r$ averages four scores and has lower observed
dispersion than the holistic grade. The larger proposal share therefore does
not establish that the criterion average is a better evaluation measure.

## Posterior predictive assessment

Posterior predictive checks used 5,000 replicated datasets to assess whether V1
reproduces the observed location, dispersion and reviewer disagreement. For
posterior draw $s$ and review $r$, let $Y_r^{\mathrm{rep},(s)}$ denote the
replicated grade,

$$
Y_r^{\mathrm{rep},(s)}
\sim
\mathcal{N}\!\left(
\bar Y
+
\theta_{p(r)}^{(s)}
+
b_{a(r)}^{(s)},
\left(\sigma^{(s)}\right)^2
\right).
$$

The observed mean absolute disagreement between the two reviews of a proposal
was 1.095, compared with a posterior predictive mean of 1.064. Approximately
40% of replicated datasets produced at least as much mean disagreement as
observed, so the observed value is not unusual under V1.

A more detailed check showed that this close correspondence is not mechanically
induced by the shared proposal effect, which cancels when the two reviews of a
proposal are differenced. The resulting analytic expected disagreement was
1.066, close to the simulated value 1.064, and most model-implied disagreement
arises from residual review-level variation rather than persistent reviewer
effects.
Mapping replicated grades to the observed integer-valued 1--5 grid did not
improve agreement for mean absolute disagreement, but substantially reduced the
apparent discrepancy in the proportion of proposals with disagreement of at
least two score points: the corresponding posterior predictive probability
increased from 0.0088 to 0.272. Full derivations and diagnostics are given in
@sec-app-disagreement.

The Gaussian likelihood also permits grades outside the admissible range: on
average, 6.6% of replicated grades were below 1 or above 5. V1 is therefore
retained as a continuous approximation for ranking latent proposal effects,
rather than as a literal generative model for valid future score categories.

![Posterior predictive checks for V1. Histograms show statistics calculated
from replicated datasets, while dashed vertical lines show the corresponding
observed values.](figures/validation/v1_posterior_predictive_checks.png){#fig-v1-ppc width=90% fig-pos="H"}

## Prior sensitivity

The baseline scale priors

$$
\sigma,\tau_\theta,\tau_b\sim\operatorname{Uniform}(0,2)
$$

were replaced by independent $\operatorname{HalfNormal}(0,1)$ priors. This
follows the suggestion of Heyard et al. [-@heyard2022] that half-normal priors
provide a useful alternative specification for variance parameters. The
$\operatorname{HalfNormal}(0,1)$ distribution is positive and unbounded,
places more prior mass near small scale values, and still allows values above 2.
It therefore provides a meaningfully different prior shape for the sensitivity
analysis.

The ranking was essentially unchanged. The Pearson correlation between
expected ranks under the two prior specifications was 0.99994, the mean
absolute expected-rank change was 0.093 positions, and the maximum was 0.283.
The median width of the 90% posterior rank intervals remained 37 under both
specifications. Additional parameter and ranking summaries are provided in
@sec-app-prior.

## Validation conclusion

V1 showed stable posterior computation, reproduced the observed mean,
dispersion and mean reviewer disagreement reasonably well, and was insensitive
to the alternative scale priors tested here. Most fitted variation was
associated with residual review-level variation, while exact proposal ranks
remained weakly identified. The principal model-form limitation is the
continuous Gaussian treatment of the five-point score, which permits replicated
values outside the admissible range. Subject to this approximation and the
non-random reviewer assignment, V1 is retained as the working model for the
review-design analysis.

# Graph-based review design

## Motivation and scope

The preceding analysis shows substantial uncertainty in the exact latent
proposal ranking. Because each proposal received only two reviews, the
reviewer--proposal assignment structure determines which proposal and reviewer
effects are jointly informed by the observed grades.

Reviewer allocation can itself be viewed as a statistical-design problem.
Cook et al. [-@cook2005] study proposal allocation with the aim of facilitating
ranking, while Stelmakh, Shah and Singh [-@stelmakh2021] consider fairness and
statistical accuracy in peer-review assignment. Osting, Brune and Osher
[-@osting2014] study targeted additions to an existing ranking graph, and
Simpson and Roberts [-@simpsonroberts2015] provide a Bayesian example of
selecting informative agent--task assignments. These settings differ from CRS,
but motivate treating additional reviews as an information-design problem.

The present analysis does not assess whether the original CRS assignments were
appropriate. They were based on expertise and availability, while detailed
eligibility and conflict-of-interest information is unavailable. Instead, the
observed assignment structure is used to ask which hypothetical additional
reviews would reduce posterior uncertainty under V1.

The analysis first compares individual additional assignments using established
A-, D- and E-optimality criteria. The primary A-optimality criterion is then
extended to small review budgets to compare random, disagreement-targeted and
sequential model-based allocation.

## Reviewer--proposal assignment structure

The CRS assignment structure can be represented as a bipartite graph: its
vertices form two groups, proposals and reviewers, and every edge joins a
proposal to a reviewer.

This is analogous to the Levi, or incidence, graph of an incomplete block
design [@baileycameron2011]. Proposals play the role of treatments and
reviewers the role of blocks, with an edge indicating that a reviewer evaluated
a proposal.

Formally,

$$
G=(P\cup R,E),
\qquad
P=\{P_1,\ldots,P_{42}\},
\qquad
R=\{R_1,\ldots,R_9\},
$$

with $(P_i,R_j)\in E$ whenever reviewer $j$ evaluated proposal $i$. Hence,

$$
|P|=42,\qquad |R|=9,\qquad |E|=84.
$$

The degree of a vertex is its number of incident edges. Every proposal has
degree two, while reviewer degrees equal their workloads and range from 6 to
12.

A subset of the observed graph is shown in @fig-review-assignment-graph to
illustrate the bipartite structure.

![Illustrative subset of the CRS reviewer--proposal assignment graph. Reviewer
vertices are shown on the left and proposal vertices on the right; each edge
represents one completed review.](figures/review_design/reviewer_proposal_graph_subset.png){#fig-review-assignment-graph width=82% fig-pos="H"}

The graph records only which reviews occurred, not the grades assigned. It
therefore represents the design of the evaluation separately from its observed
outcomes.

## Statistical relevance of the assignment structure

The graph is statistically relevant because incidence matrices and graph
Laplacians arise directly in the information matrices of incomplete block
designs. Bailey and Cameron [-@baileycameron2011] show this connection for an
additive treatment--block model. V1 has an analogous crossed structure, with
proposal effects replacing treatment effects and reviewer effects replacing
block effects.

To obtain the standard signed incidence representation, define

$$
c_j=-b_j.
$$

Here $c_j$ is only a sign-transformed reviewer effect; it does not denote a
graph connection. An observed grade from reviewer $j$ for proposal $i$ can then
be written as

$$
Y_{ij}-\bar Y
=
\theta_i-c_j+\varepsilon_{ij}.
$$

Collect the effects into

$$
\beta
=
(\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_{42},c_1,\ldots,c_9)^\top.
$$

For edge $e=(i,j)$, let $x_e$ be the oriented incidence vector with $+1$ at
proposal $i$, $-1$ at reviewer $j$, and zero elsewhere. Stacking the 84 vectors
gives the incidence matrix $X$. Let
$Y=(Y_1,\ldots,Y_{84})^\top$ denote the vector of observed grades and
$\mathbf 1\in\mathbb R^{84}$ the vector of ones. Then

$$
Y-\bar Y\mathbf 1
=
X\beta+\varepsilon.
$$

For an oriented incidence matrix,

$$
X^\top X=L_G,
$$

where $L_G$ is the graph Laplacian: diagonal entries are vertex degrees and
off-diagonal entries are $-1$ for connected proposal--reviewer pairs and zero
otherwise.

Conditional on $\tau_\theta$, $\tau_b$ and $\sigma$, the prior precision for
$\beta$ is

$$
P_0
=
\begin{pmatrix}
\tau_\theta^{-2}I_{42} & 0_{42\times9}\\
0_{9\times42} & \tau_b^{-2}I_9
\end{pmatrix}.
$$
The zero off-diagonal blocks reflect prior independence between the proposal and
reviewer effects.

The conditional posterior precision and covariance are therefore

$$
Q
=
P_0+\frac{1}{\sigma^2}L_G,
\qquad
V=Q^{-1}.
$$

The assignment graph thus enters directly into posterior precision: changing an
edge changes $L_G$ and therefore the conditional posterior covariance. A full
derivation is given in @sec-app-graph-model.

## Quantifying uncertainty for review design {#sec-review-design-criteria}

The statistical value of an additional review depends on how uncertainty is
defined. Rather than introducing a CRS-specific measure, the analysis uses
A-, D- and E-optimality, established criteria in experimental design
[@baileycameron2011; @osting2014].

Because ranking depends on differences between proposal effects, uncertainty is
evaluated on proposal contrasts. Let $V_\theta$ denote the $42\times42$
proposal-effect block of $V$. For proposals $i$ and $k$,

$$
\operatorname{Var}(\theta_i-\theta_k\mid Y)
=
(e_i-e_k)^\top V_\theta(e_i-e_k),
$$

where $e_i$ is the $i$th standard basis vector.

The primary **A-optimality** loss is the average variance of all pairwise
proposal contrasts,

$$
L_A(V_\theta)
=
\frac{2}{42\cdot41}
\sum_{i<k}
(e_i-e_k)^\top V_\theta(e_i-e_k).
$$

Smaller values therefore indicate greater average precision in pairwise
proposal comparisons.

For the alternative criteria, define the centering matrix

$$
H
=
I_{42}
-
\frac{1}{42}\mathbf 1\mathbf 1^\top,
$$

where $\mathbf 1\in\mathbb R^{42}$ is the vector of ones. The matrix $HV_\theta H$ represents covariance on the proposal-contrast
subspace. Because $H$ projects out the common-shift direction,
$HV_\theta H$ has one zero eigenvalue and 41 non-zero eigenvalues
$\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_{41}$.

The **D-optimality** loss is

$$
L_D(V_\theta)
=
\sum_{\ell=1}^{41}\log(\lambda_\ell)
=
\log\operatorname{pdet}(HV_\theta H),
$$

where $\operatorname{pdet}$ is the product of the non-zero eigenvalues. It
measures global joint uncertainty in the proposal-contrast space.

The **E-optimality** loss is

$$
L_E(V_\theta)
=
\lambda_{\max}(HV_\theta H),
$$

which targets the least precisely estimated normalized contrast direction.

A-optimality is primary because proposal ranking depends directly on pairwise
contrasts. D- and E-optimality provide sensitivity to different notions of
uncertainty: joint uncertainty and worst-case contrast uncertainty,
respectively.

Classical block-design theory compares complete designs, whereas the CRS design
is already observed. The present problem therefore considers one-edge
augmentations $G+e$ of the existing graph, analogous to targeted augmentation
of an existing ranking design [@osting2014].

## Statistical value of a single additional review {#sec-single-review-design}

There are

$$
42\times9-84=294
$$

currently unobserved reviewer--proposal pairs. Because expertise, eligibility
and conflict-of-interest information is unavailable, all 294 are treated as
hypothetical candidates; their rankings describe statistical informativeness
under V1 rather than operational assignment recommendations.

The calculation propagates uncertainty in the scale parameters by evaluating
each candidate over 5,000 approximately evenly spaced posterior draws from V1.
For draw $s$, the matrices in the preceding sections are evaluated at
$\tau_\theta^{(s)}$, $\tau_b^{(s)}$ and $\sigma^{(s)}$, giving covariance
$V^{(s)}$.

For a candidate edge $e$ with incidence vector $x_e$, adding the review changes
the graph Laplacian by

$$
L_{G+e}
=
L_G+x_ex_e^\top.
$$

The resulting rank-one precision update gives, by the Sherman--Morrison
identity,

$$
V_e^{(s)}
=
V^{(s)}
-
\frac{
V^{(s)}x_ex_e^\top V^{(s)}
}{
\left(\sigma^{(s)}\right)^2
+
x_e^\top V^{(s)}x_e
}.
$$

Let $V_\theta^{(s)}$ and $V_{\theta,e}^{(s)}$ denote the
$42\times42$ proposal-effect blocks of $V^{(s)}$ and $V_e^{(s)}$,
respectively.

Conditional on the scale parameters, the covariance reduction therefore
depends on the assignment added, not on the future numerical grade.

For criterion $C\in\{A,D,E\}$, define

$$
\Delta_C^{(s)}(e)
=
L_C\!\left(V_\theta^{(s)}\right)
-
L_C\!\left(V_{\theta,e}^{(s)}\right),
$$

and average over posterior draws,

$$
\overline{\Delta}_C(e)
=
\frac{1}{S}
\sum_{s=1}^{S}
\Delta_C^{(s)}(e).
$$

Larger values indicate a greater posterior-averaged reduction in uncertainty.
A 1,000-draw calculation gave materially similar highest-ranked assignments,
supporting the use of 5,000 draws in the final analysis.

As a further sensitivity check, posterior-median plug-in scale parameters
produced broadly similar candidate rankings and the same five highest-ranked
A-optimal assignments as a set. Detailed results are given in
@sec-app-review-design-sensitivity.

This is not a full prospective refit of V1. Within each posterior draw, the
scale parameters remain fixed; an actually observed additional grade could also
update their posterior distributions.

## Comparison of single-review criteria

The posterior-averaged calculation identified a small group of assignments with
almost identical A-optimality utility. P026--R02 gave the largest reduction,

$$
\overline{\Delta}_A
=
3.0535\times10^{-4},
$$

followed by P005--R02 and P015--R02 at
$3.0534\times10^{-4}$. These differences are too small to support a meaningful
distinction between the three assignments.

D-optimality produced a similar upper ordering, whereas E-optimality differed
more substantially. Across all 294 candidates,

$$
\rho_{\mathrm S}(A,D)=0.926,
\qquad
\rho_{\mathrm S}(A,E)=0.234,
\qquad
\rho_{\mathrm S}(D,E)=0.040.
$$

Thus, A- and D-optimality agree strongly about candidate assignments, while the
worst-direction criterion represented by E-optimality gives a different
ordering.

| Candidate assignment | A rank | D rank | E rank |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| P026--R02 | 1 | 1 | 18 |
| P005--R02 | 2 | 3 | 1 |
| P015--R02 | 3 | 2 | 2 |
| P032--R02 | 4 | 4 | 5 |
| P029--R02 | 4 | 5 | 6 |
| P034--R02 | 4 | 5 | 7 |
| P005--R03 | 8 | 41 | 3 |
| P015--R03 | 9 | 42 | 4 |

: Selected highest-ranked candidate assignments under the posterior-averaged A-, D- and E-optimality criteria. {#tbl-single-review-candidates}

The full A-optimality pattern is shown in @fig-review-design-heatmap. High
utilities are concentrated among assignments involving R02, but this reflects
the assignment structure and covariance model and should not be interpreted as
evidence about reviewer quality.

![Posterior-averaged A-optimality utility for hypothetical additional
reviewer--proposal assignments. Grey cells indicate existing assignments;
outlined cells form the highest-ranked A-optimality group. Larger values
indicate greater reductions in average pairwise proposal-contrast
variance.](figures/review_design/a_optimality_candidate_heatmap.png){#fig-review-design-heatmap width=82% fig-pos="H"}

Targeting proposals with high observed reviewer disagreement addresses a
different objective. It prioritizes proposals whose original reviewers gave
divergent judgments, whereas A-optimality reduces global posterior contrast
uncertainty. This motivates the disagreement-targeted benchmark considered
next.

## Practical comparison of limited-review allocation policies

The single-review calculation was extended to budgets of one to six additional
reviews. Each proposal could receive at most one additional review, so the
policies allocate selective third reviews.

The **random policy** selects an available reviewer--proposal assignment
uniformly at random. The **disagreement-targeted policy** selects among
proposals that have not yet received an additional review and have the highest
absolute difference between their two original grades, then chooses the
available reviewer edge with the largest A-optimality reduction within that
group. The **sequential A-optimal policy** instead chooses the globally best
remaining edge at each step and updates the covariance before selecting the
next edge. This procedure is greedy and is not claimed to identify the jointly
optimal set of reviews.

For policy $\pi$ and budget $m$, define the posterior-averaged cumulative
A-optimality reduction as

$$
\overline{\Delta}_A(m;\pi)
=
\frac{1}{S}
\sum_{s=1}^{S}
\left[
L_A\!\left(V_{\theta,0}^{(s)}\right)
-
L_A\!\left(V_{\theta,m,\pi}^{(s)}\right)
\right].
$$

Relative to the baseline uncertainty,

$$
G_m(\pi)
=
100
\frac{
\overline{\Delta}_A(m;\pi)
}{
\overline{L}_A(0)
},
\qquad
\overline{L}_A(0)
=
\frac{1}{S}
\sum_{s=1}^{S}
L_A\!\left(V_{\theta,0}^{(s)}\right).
$$

The sequential policies were evaluated over 5,000 posterior draws, while the
random benchmark used 5,000 simulated allocation paths with fixed seed
20260823, balanced across the same draws.

At six additional reviews, average pairwise proposal-contrast variance was
reduced by 1.609% under sequential A-optimal allocation, 1.604% under
disagreement-targeted allocation and 1.592% under random allocation. The three
policies therefore produced almost identical reductions in the global
A-optimality criterion throughout the examined budget range.

![Posterior-averaged reduction in average pairwise proposal-contrast variance
under random, disagreement-targeted and sequential A-optimal allocation of up
to six additional reviews. Each proposal can receive at most one additional
review.](figures/review_design/review_policy_comparison.png){#fig-review-policy-comparison width=86% fig-pos="H"}

At six reviews, sequential A-optimal allocation exceeded the random benchmark
by only 0.017 percentage points. Thus, under V1 and this global uncertainty
criterion, optimizing the exact placement of a small number of additional
reviews provides little improvement over random supplementation in the present
CRS design.

This result concerns global A-optimality, not all possible notions of ranking
uncertainty. The disagreement-targeted policy deliberately addresses a
different substantive objective by concentrating additional opinions on
proposals whose original reviewers disagreed.

## Generalization beyond the CRS design

The matrix formulation applies more generally to crossed reviewer--proposal
models with an additive Gaussian information structure, although candidate
utilities will depend on the assignment graph, fitted variance components and
chosen uncertainty criterion.

The present multi-review comparison uses a greedy sequential update rather than
joint optimization, and the disagreement-targeted policy retains the
disagreement observed in the original two reviews rather than updating it after
a hypothetical third grade. A prospective implementation would also restrict
candidate assignments according to expertise, conflicts of interest, workload
and availability. A fully adaptive Bayesian design could then observe each new
grade, update the hierarchical model and choose the next assignment.

# Discussion and recommendations

## Answers to the research questions

**Research Question 1.** Under V1, P022, P032, P023 and P041 occupied the
first four posterior-mean positions, with expected ranks from 13.08 to 16.22.
Their 90% posterior rank intervals nevertheless extended to ranks 36--38,
showing substantial uncertainty in the exact latent ordering.

**Research Question 2.** The four proposals satisfying the CRS qualification
rule were also the first four by posterior-mean V1 effect. The Bayesian model
therefore did not change the group identified by the final rule, but quantified
substantial uncertainty that the coarse observed-score ranking, with many ties,
does not show directly.

**Research Question 3.** V1 showed stable MCMC computation, reproduced the
observed mean, dispersion and mean reviewer disagreement reasonably well, and
showed negligible ranking sensitivity to the alternative scale priors. Its
principal model-form limitation is the continuous Gaussian treatment of the
integer 1--5 score, which produced about 6.6% of replicated grades outside the
admissible range.

**Research Question 4.** Scientific quality was the criterion most strongly
associated with the holistic overall grade. Replacing that grade by an
equal-weight criterion average changed the Bayesian ordering substantially more
than changing from V0 to V1: the expected-rank correlation between the two V1
outcomes was 0.863, and only three of the four original qualifiers remained in
the criterion-average posterior-mean top four. This demonstrates sensitivity to
outcome definition without establishing that either outcome is preferable.

**Research Question 5.** Under A-optimality, P026--R02, P005--R02 and
P015--R02 formed an almost tied highest-value group. A- and D-optimality gave
similar candidate rankings ($\rho_{\mathrm S}=0.926$), whereas E-optimality
produced a substantially different ordering, showing that the preferred
additional review depends on the uncertainty criterion.

As a practical extension, random, disagreement-targeted and sequential
A-optimal allocation were compared for up to six additional reviews. Their
reductions in the global A-optimality criterion were nearly identical: 1.592%,
1.604% and 1.609%, respectively, at a budget of six reviews.

## Interpretation of the main findings

The central result is not a different set of leading proposals produced by the
Bayesian model. The final CRS qualifiers also occupy the first four
posterior-mean V1 positions, while the posterior distributions show that the
exact latent ordering is weakly identified. This is consistent with the fitted
variance structure, in which proposal-level variation is small relative to
residual review-level variation.

Two different forms of sensitivity should be distinguished. Simplifying the
Heyard reference model from V0 to V1 changes the ranking very little, whereas
changing the evaluation outcome from the holistic grade to an equal-weight
criterion average has a noticeably larger effect. In the analyses considered
here, the definition of what is being ranked therefore matters more than the
difference between the two hierarchical model specifications.

The review-design analysis links this uncertainty to data collection. Additional
assignments can differ in their statistical information value, and the preferred
single edge depends on the uncertainty criterion. However, for the global
A-optimality objective and budgets of up to six reviews, the exact allocation
policy matters very little. This does not rule out larger differences under
other assignment structures or more decision-focused objectives.

## Implications for CRS

For future evaluations, the score used for the final decision should be
specified clearly before reviews are collected. The 2026 call described an
average across criteria and reviewers, whereas the implemented procedure used a
separate holistic overall grade. The present analysis shows that these outcome
definitions can produce meaningfully different proposal orderings.

When only a few reviews are available, fine distinctions between proposal ranks
should also be interpreted cautiously. Posterior rank intervals or selected
pairwise posterior probabilities can complement a transparent score-based
decision rule by showing how strongly the available reviews support particular
comparisons.

Additional review capacity can be treated as an explicit design choice.
However, the present global A-optimality comparison gives little reason to
adopt a complex allocation algorithm solely to improve average pairwise
precision. Other objectives may still justify selective review, for example
resolving strong reviewer disagreement or uncertainty near a decision boundary.
Any prospective allocation rule would first need to respect reviewer expertise,
conflicts of interest, workload and availability.

## Ranking uncertainty and decision making

Broad posterior rank intervals do not imply that the four funding decisions
were incorrect. The CRS rule is a deterministic qualification threshold based
on the observed grades, whereas the Bayesian model quantifies uncertainty in
the latent ordering of proposals. The same four qualifiers occupied the first
four posterior-mean V1 positions, and funding capacity was not binding. The
uncertainty result is therefore narrower: the available reviews do not support
strong claims about the exact ordering of many proposals. This distinction
would become more consequential if a future decision required a strict ranking
near a funding boundary.

## Limitations

First, the dataset is small and sparse: 42 proposals were evaluated by nine
reviewers, with only two reviews per proposal. Variance components and latent
ranks are therefore estimated from limited replication.

Second, reviewer assignment was based on expertise and availability rather than
random allocation. Reviewer effects consequently represent
reviewer-associated scoring tendencies rather than causal measures of bias.
The Chapter 6 candidate set also omits expertise, conflicts, workload and
availability constraints.

Third, the review-design calculations update conditional covariance while
holding scale parameters fixed within each posterior draw. They do not simulate
future grades or refit the complete hierarchy after each additional review. The
disagreement-targeted policy likewise uses disagreement from the original two
reviews.

Fourth, V1 models the five-point holistic grade using a homogeneous Gaussian
likelihood. This permits values outside the observed 1--5 range. The
prior-sensitivity analysis does not address this likelihood assumption, and an
ordinal model was not fitted as a formal sensitivity analysis.

Fifth, the criterion-average analysis is an equal-weight counterfactual. It
does not recover the weights reviewers implicitly used in assigning the
holistic grade and does not establish that equal weighting is preferable.

Finally, this is a retrospective analysis of one small grant call. The
qualitative findings may inform related settings, but the numerical rankings,
variance estimates and preferred additional assignments are specific to the CRS
data and fitted model.

## Future work

A natural model extension is an ordinal hierarchical specification that
respects the five observed score categories while retaining proposal and
reviewer effects. Comparing such a model with V1 would directly test whether
the continuous-score approximation affects the ranking conclusions.

For review design, future work could incorporate operational eligibility
constraints such as expertise, conflicts of interest, workload and availability,
and compare the present greedy sequential rule with joint optimization under a
fixed review budget. A fully adaptive design could observe each additional
grade, refit the Bayesian model and then choose the next assignment.
Decision-focused utilities could also target uncertainty for particular
proposals, for example those with substantial reviewer disagreement or near a
qualification boundary, rather than averaging uncertainty over all proposal
pairs.

The limited-budget comparison also raises a broader structural question: when
does graph-based targeting meaningfully outperform random supplementation?
One hypothesis is that its advantage increases when assignment graphs exhibit
strong workload imbalance, clustering or connectivity bottlenecks, particularly
when persistent reviewer variation is large relative to residual review-level
variation. An edge connecting weakly linked parts of such a graph may then
provide substantially more information than an additional review within an
already well-connected region. Simulation studies varying both graph structure
and variance components could test this hypothesis.

The strongest empirical validation would be prospective: a pre-specified
ranking and review-design procedure could be applied in a future CRS call and
its predicted information gains compared with the uncertainty observed after
additional reviews are collected.

# Conclusion

The CRS Seed Grant 2026 evaluation illustrates the uncertainty that can arise
when many proposals are assessed by only a few reviewers. The Bayesian
cross-classified model placed the four CRS qualifiers in the first four
posterior-mean positions, while showing substantial uncertainty in their exact
latent ordering. This conclusion was stable to the Heyard reference
specification and to the alternative scale priors tested here. The main
model-form limitation remains the continuous Gaussian treatment of the
five-point score.

The analysis also showed that the definition of the evaluation outcome matters.
Replacing the holistic overall grade with an equal-weight average of the four
supporting criteria changed the proposal ordering more noticeably than changing
from V0 to V1. This supports specifying clearly in advance which score or
summary is intended to drive the decision.

Finally, the reviewer--proposal assignment graph links the review design
directly to posterior uncertainty under V1. A-, D- and E-optimality provide
principled ways to evaluate hypothetical additional reviews, but for small
review budgets the precise allocation strategy had little effect on the global
A-optimality criterion in the present CRS design. The broader practical
conclusion is therefore to combine transparent decision rules with explicit
uncertainty summaries and to define clearly what additional review effort is
intended to resolve before choosing an allocation strategy.

# Supplementary methods and analyses {.appendix}

## Correlation definitions {#sec-app-correlation}

For criterion $c$, the sample Pearson correlation with the holistic overall grade is

$$
\operatorname{Cor}_{\mathrm P}(C_{\cdot c},Y)
=
\frac{
\sum_{r=1}^{n}(C_{rc}-\bar C_c)(Y_r-\bar Y)
}{
\sqrt{
\sum_{r=1}^{n}(C_{rc}-\bar C_c)^2
\sum_{r=1}^{n}(Y_r-\bar Y)^2
}
},
$$

where $n=84$,
$C_{\cdot c}=(C_{1c},\ldots,C_{nc})^\top$ and
$Y=(Y_1,\ldots,Y_n)^\top$. The corresponding sample Spearman correlation is

$$
\operatorname{Cor}_{\mathrm S}(C_{\cdot c},Y)
=
\operatorname{Cor}_{\mathrm P}\!\left(R(C_{\cdot c}),R(Y)\right),
$$

where $R(\cdot)$ denotes the rank transformation and average ranks are used for
ties.

## Bayesian updating and partial pooling in V1 {#sec-app-bayesian-updating}

This section gives a mathematical explanation of how the observed grades
inform the proposal and reviewer effects in V1, making the Bayesian updating
mechanism and resulting partial pooling explicit.

### From the model to the posterior distribution

Recall that V1 represents review $r$ as

$$
Y_r
=
\bar Y
+
\theta_{p(r)}
+
b_{a(r)}
+
\varepsilon_r,
\qquad
\varepsilon_r\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^2),
$$

where $\theta_i$ is the latent effect of proposal $i$, $b_j$ is the effect of
reviewer $j$, and $\sigma^2$ is the residual review-level variance. The
hierarchical distributions are

$$
\theta_i\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\tau_\theta^2),
\qquad
b_j\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\tau_b^2).
$$

For given values of the model parameters, the density of one observed grade is

$$
p(Y_r\mid\theta,b,\sigma)
=
\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}}
\exp\!\left[
-\frac{
\left(
Y_r-\bar Y-\theta_{p(r)}-b_{a(r)}
\right)^2
}{
2\sigma^2
}
\right].
$$

Conditional on the model parameters, the review-level residuals are assumed
independent. The likelihood of the complete observed dataset
$Y=(Y_1,\ldots,Y_{84})^\top$ is therefore

$$
p(Y\mid\theta,b,\sigma)
=
\prod_{r=1}^{84}
p(Y_r\mid\theta,b,\sigma).
$$

Bayes' theorem combines this likelihood with the prior distributions. For all
unknown quantities together,

$$
p(\theta,b,\tau_\theta,\tau_b,\sigma\mid Y)
=
\frac{
p(Y\mid\theta,b,\sigma)\,
p(\theta,b,\tau_\theta,\tau_b,\sigma)
}{
p(Y)
}.
$$

Since the denominator $p(Y)$ does not depend on the unknown parameters, the
same relationship can be written as

$$
p(\theta,b,\tau_\theta,\tau_b,\sigma\mid Y)
\propto
p(Y\mid\theta,b,\sigma)\,
p(\theta,b,\tau_\theta,\tau_b,\sigma),
$$

where $\propto$ means "proportional to". Using the hierarchical structure of
V1 gives

$$
p(\theta,b,\tau_\theta,\tau_b,\sigma\mid Y)
\propto
p(Y\mid\theta,b,\sigma)
\left[
\prod_{i=1}^{42}p(\theta_i\mid\tau_\theta)
\right]
\left[
\prod_{j=1}^{9}p(b_j\mid\tau_b)
\right]
p(\tau_\theta)p(\tau_b)p(\sigma).
$$

The posterior therefore combines the information in the observed grades,
through the likelihood, with the hierarchical prior distributions.

### Updating one proposal effect

The partial-pooling mechanism can be seen explicitly by considering one
proposal $i$. Let

$$
\mathcal{R}_i
=
\{r:p(r)=i\}
$$

denote the set of reviews received by proposal $i$, and define

$$
n_i
=
|\mathcal{R}_i|.
$$

Thus, $n_i$ is simply the number of reviews received by proposal $i$. In the
CRS data,

$$
n_i=2
$$

for every proposal.

To make the updating calculation transparent, suppose temporarily that the
reviewer effects $b$, the residual variance $\sigma^2$, and the
between-proposal variance $\tau_\theta^2$ are known.

For a review $r\in\mathcal{R}_i$, define the reviewer-adjusted grade

$$
Z_r
=
Y_r-\bar Y-b_{a(r)}.
$$

Conditional on the assumed reviewer effects, this removes the reviewer-specific
component from the observed grade.

Substituting the V1 model gives

$$
Z_r
=
\theta_i+\varepsilon_r,
\qquad
\varepsilon_r\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^2),
$$

and therefore

$$
Z_r\mid\theta_i
\sim
\mathcal{N}(\theta_i,\sigma^2).
$$

The likelihood for $\theta_i$ based on its $n_i$ adjusted grades is

$$
p(Z_i\mid\theta_i,\sigma)
=
\prod_{r\in\mathcal{R}_i}
p(Z_r\mid\theta_i,\sigma),
$$

where $Z_i$ denotes the collection of adjusted grades for proposal $i$.
Ignoring multiplicative constants that do not depend on $\theta_i$,

$$
p(Z_i\mid\theta_i,\sigma)
\propto
\exp\!\left[
-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}
\sum_{r\in\mathcal{R}_i}
(Z_r-\theta_i)^2
\right].
$$

The prior distribution

$$
\theta_i\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\tau_\theta^2)
$$

has density, again ignoring constants independent of $\theta_i$,

$$
p(\theta_i\mid\tau_\theta)
\propto
\exp\!\left(
-\frac{\theta_i^2}{2\tau_\theta^2}
\right).
$$

Bayes' theorem gives

$$
p(\theta_i\mid Z_i,\sigma,\tau_\theta)
\propto
p(Z_i\mid\theta_i,\sigma)\,
p(\theta_i\mid\tau_\theta),
$$

so

$$
p(\theta_i\mid Z_i,\sigma,\tau_\theta)
\propto
\exp\!\left[
-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}
\sum_{r\in\mathcal{R}_i}
(Z_r-\theta_i)^2
-\frac{\theta_i^2}{2\tau_\theta^2}
\right].
$$

To identify this posterior distribution, expand the square:

$$
\sum_{r\in\mathcal{R}_i}(Z_r-\theta_i)^2
=
\sum_{r\in\mathcal{R}_i}Z_r^2
-
2\theta_i
\sum_{r\in\mathcal{R}_i}Z_r
+
n_i\theta_i^2.
$$

The term $\sum Z_r^2$ does not depend on $\theta_i$ and can therefore be
absorbed into the proportionality constant. The remaining terms give

$$
p(\theta_i\mid Z_i,\sigma,\tau_\theta)
\propto
\exp\!\left[
-\frac{1}{2}
\left\{
\left(
\frac{n_i}{\sigma^2}
+
\frac{1}{\tau_\theta^2}
\right)\theta_i^2
-
2
\left(
\frac{
\sum_{r\in\mathcal{R}_i}Z_r
}{
\sigma^2
}
\right)\theta_i
\right\}
\right].
$$

A normal density with mean $\mu_i^{(\theta)}$ and variance
$v_i^{(\theta)}$ has the same quadratic form,

$$
\exp\!\left[
-\frac{1}{2v_i^{(\theta)}}
\left(
\theta_i-\mu_i^{(\theta)}
\right)^2
\right].
$$

Expanding this square and comparing coefficients gives

$$
\frac{1}{v_i^{(\theta)}}
=
\frac{1}{\tau_\theta^2}
+
\frac{n_i}{\sigma^2},
$$

and therefore

$$
v_i^{(\theta)}
=
\left(
\frac{1}{\tau_\theta^2}
+
\frac{n_i}{\sigma^2}
\right)^{-1}.
$$

The coefficient of $\theta_i$ gives

$$
\frac{\mu_i^{(\theta)}}{v_i^{(\theta)}}
=
\frac{
\sum_{r\in\mathcal{R}_i}Z_r
}{
\sigma^2
},
$$

so

$$
\mu_i^{(\theta)}
=
v_i^{(\theta)}
\frac{
\sum_{r\in\mathcal{R}_i}Z_r
}{
\sigma^2
}.
$$

Now define the mean reviewer-adjusted grade for proposal $i$ as

$$
\bar Z_i
=
\frac{1}{n_i}
\sum_{r\in\mathcal{R}_i}Z_r.
$$

Since

$$
\sum_{r\in\mathcal{R}_i}Z_r
=
n_i\bar Z_i,
$$

the posterior mean simplifies to

$$
\mu_i^{(\theta)}
=
\frac{
n_i\tau_\theta^2
}{
\sigma^2+n_i\tau_\theta^2
}
\bar Z_i.
$$

Thus,

$$
\theta_i\mid Z_i,\sigma,\tau_\theta
\sim
\mathcal{N}
\left(
\mu_i^{(\theta)},
v_i^{(\theta)}
\right).
$$

### Partial pooling

Define the shrinkage factor

$$
\kappa_i
=
\frac{
n_i\tau_\theta^2
}{
\sigma^2+n_i\tau_\theta^2
}.
$$

Because all variance terms are positive,

$$
0<\kappa_i<1.
$$

The conditional posterior mean can therefore be written as

$$
\mu_i^{(\theta)}
=
\kappa_i\bar Z_i.
$$

The reviewer-adjusted observed mean $\bar Z_i$ is consequently pulled toward
the prior mean zero rather than being used directly as the estimate of the
proposal effect. This is the partial-pooling mechanism.

The amount of pooling is governed by $\kappa_i$. More reviews increase
$n_i$ and therefore give the observed grades more influence. Larger residual
variation $\sigma^2$ decreases $\kappa_i$ and produces stronger shrinkage,
because individual reviews are treated as noisier. Larger between-proposal
variation $\tau_\theta^2$ increases $\kappa_i$, allowing proposal effects to
remain further away from zero.

For the CRS design, $n_i=2$ for every proposal, so

$$
\kappa_i
=
\frac{
2\tau_\theta^2
}{
\sigma^2+2\tau_\theta^2
}.
$$

Since $\theta_i=0$ corresponds to a proposal whose expected grade equals the
overall mean $\bar Y$, shrinking $\theta_i$ toward zero corresponds to shrinking
the proposal's fitted grade toward the overall evaluation mean.

### Updating reviewer effects

Reviewer effects are updated in the same way. Let

$$
\mathcal{S}_j
=
\{r:a(r)=j\}
$$

denote the set of reviews completed by reviewer $j$, and define

$$
d_j
=
|\mathcal{S}_j|.
$$

Thus, $d_j$ is the number of reviews completed by reviewer $j$.

Suppose temporarily that the proposal effects $\theta$, the residual variance
$\sigma^2$, and the between-reviewer variance $\tau_b^2$ are known. Define the
proposal-adjusted grade

$$
W_r
=
Y_r-\bar Y-\theta_{p(r)}.
$$

For reviews completed by reviewer $j$,

$$
W_r
=
b_j+\varepsilon_r,
$$

so

$$
W_r\mid b_j
\sim
\mathcal{N}(b_j,\sigma^2).
$$

Combining these observations with the prior

$$
b_j\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\tau_b^2)
$$

and applying the same normal--normal calculation gives

$$
b_j\mid Y,\theta,\sigma,\tau_b
\sim
\mathcal{N}
\left(
\mu_j^{(b)},
v_j^{(b)}
\right),
$$

where

$$
v_j^{(b)}
=
\left(
\frac{1}{\tau_b^2}
+
\frac{d_j}{\sigma^2}
\right)^{-1}.
$$

Define the mean proposal-adjusted grade assigned by reviewer $j$ as

$$
\bar W_j
=
\frac{1}{d_j}
\sum_{r\in\mathcal{S}_j}W_r.
$$

The conditional posterior mean is then

$$
\mu_j^{(b)}
=
\frac{
d_j\tau_b^2
}{
\sigma^2+d_j\tau_b^2
}
\bar W_j.
$$

Thus, the several proposals assessed by the same reviewer jointly inform that
reviewer's scoring tendency. Reviewers with more observed reviews are, all else
equal, subject to less shrinkage toward zero.

### From the joint posterior to proposal ranks

The calculations above treat some quantities as known only to make the updating
mechanism visible. In the fitted V1 model, the proposal effects, reviewer
effects, $\tau_\theta$, $\tau_b$, and $\sigma$ are all unknown and are estimated
jointly. Their posterior distributions therefore depend on one another.

JAGS uses Markov chain Monte Carlo to generate draws from this joint posterior.
A retained posterior draw $s$ contains

$$
\left(
\theta_1^{(s)},\ldots,\theta_{42}^{(s)},
b_1^{(s)},\ldots,b_9^{(s)},
\tau_\theta^{(s)},
\tau_b^{(s)},
\sigma^{(s)}
\right).
$$

Each draw represents one set of parameter values compatible with the observed
grades and the model assumptions. The proposal effects within that draw,

$$
\theta_1^{(s)},\ldots,\theta_{42}^{(s)},
$$

are ordered from largest to smallest to obtain one possible proposal ranking.
Repeating this calculation across posterior draws produces the posterior rank
distributions described in Section 3.5.

The Bayesian ranking therefore follows the sequence

$$
\text{observed grades}
\longrightarrow
\text{posterior proposal and reviewer effects}
\longrightarrow
\text{posterior proposal ranks}.
$$

Partial pooling enters before the ranking step: the limited and noisy review
information is combined with the hierarchical model before the proposal effects
are ranked.

## V0 reference-model details {#sec-app-v0}

Under V0, P022 had posterior-mean rank 1 and expected rank 11.85. P023, P032 and P041 occupied posterior-mean ranks 2, 3 and 4, with expected ranks 15.45, 15.49 and 16.50. Their 90% posterior rank intervals were 1--35, 1--37, 1--37 and 2--38, respectively. The maximum PSRF across monitored V0 parameters was 1.0077 and the minimum effective sample size was 501.

For completeness, @fig-v0-ranking-comparison shows the comparison between the observed-score rank, posterior-mean rank and expected rank under V0.

![Proposal rankings under the observed-score ranking, posterior-mean ranking and posterior expected rank for the V0 Heyard reference model.](figures/model_comparison/ranking_comparison_V0.png){#fig-v0-ranking-comparison width=95% fig-pos="H"}

## V1 MCMC trace plots {#sec-app-trace}

@fig-v1-trace shows the final 5,000 retained iterations from each V1 chain,
plotting every fifth value for readability. Numerical diagnostics in the main
text are based on the full posterior sample.

![Trace plots for the V1 scale parameters $\tau_\theta$, $\tau_b$, and $\sigma$.](figures/validation/v1_trace_plots.png){#fig-v1-trace width=88% fig-pos="H"}

## Detailed reviewer-disagreement diagnostic {#sec-app-disagreement}

Consider proposal $i$, reviewed by reviewers $j$ and $k$. Under V1,

$$
Y_{ij}-Y_{ik}
=
b_j-b_k+\varepsilon_{ij}-\varepsilon_{ik},
$$

so the proposal effect cancels and

$$
Y_{ij}-Y_{ik}\mid b_j,b_k,\sigma
\sim
\mathcal{N}(b_j-b_k,2\sigma^2).
$$

Taking the absolute value gives a folded normal distribution [@tsagris2014]. If $X\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu,s^2)$, then

$$
\operatorname{E}|X|
=
s\sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi}}
\exp\!\left(-\frac{\mu^2}{2s^2}\right)
+
|\mu|
\left[
2\Phi\!\left(\frac{|\mu|}{s}\right)-1
\right],
$$

where $\Phi$ is the standard normal cumulative distribution function. In the present setting, $\mu=b_j-b_k$ and $s=\sqrt{2}\sigma$. Evaluating this expression for the observed reviewer pairs and posterior draws gave analytic posterior mean disagreement 1.066, almost identical to the simulated posterior predictive mean 1.064. The posterior predictive probability of mean disagreement at least as large as the observed value 1.095 was 0.401.

Most of the model-implied disagreement is associated with residual review-level variation. If the two reviewer effects are equal, the expected absolute disagreement simplifies to

$$
\operatorname{E}|Y_{ij}-Y_{ik}|
=
\frac{2\sigma}{\sqrt{\pi}},
$$

which averaged 1.043 over the posterior. Allowing the fitted reviewer effects to differ increased the expected mean disagreement by only about 0.023 on average.

A threshold-based check gave a less favourable result. Observed absolute
disagreement was 0 for 10 proposals, 1 for 19 proposals, 2 for 12 proposals
and 3 for one proposal. Thus, 13 of 42 proposals had disagreement of at least
two score points, giving

$$
T_{\mathrm{obs}}
=
\frac{13}{42}
\approx0.310.
$$

Let $T_{\mathrm{cont}}^{\mathrm{rep}}$ denote the corresponding proportion
calculated from a continuous Gaussian replicated dataset. Its posterior
predictive mean was 0.134, and

$$
\mathbb{P}
\left(
T_{\mathrm{cont}}^{\mathrm{rep}}
\ge
T_{\mathrm{obs}}
\mid Y
\right)
=
0.0088.
$$

Because the observed scores are integer-valued, each replicated grade was also
mapped diagnostically to the 1--5 grid,

$$
\widetilde Y_r^{\mathrm{rep}}
=
\min\left\{
5,
\max\left\{
1,
\operatorname{round}(Y_r^{\mathrm{rep}})
\right\}
\right\}.
$$

Let $T_{\mathrm{disc}}^{\mathrm{rep}}$ denote the proportion of proposals with
disagreement of at least two points after this transformation. Its posterior
predictive mean increased to 0.255, and

$$
\mathbb{P}
\left(
T_{\mathrm{disc}}^{\mathrm{rep}}
\ge
T_{\mathrm{obs}}
\mid Y
\right)
=
0.272.
$$

The same transformation did not improve agreement for mean absolute
disagreement. Let $D_{\mathrm{obs}}=1.095$ denote the observed mean absolute
disagreement and let $D_{\mathrm{disc}}^{\mathrm{rep}}$ denote the corresponding
statistic calculated from a grid-mapped replicated dataset. Its posterior
predictive mean was 1.020, compared with 1.064 under continuous Gaussian
replication. The 95% posterior predictive interval for
$D_{\mathrm{disc}}^{\mathrm{rep}}$ was approximately $[0.738,1.333]$, and

$$
\mathbb{P}
\left(
D_{\mathrm{disc}}^{\mathrm{rep}}
\ge
D_{\mathrm{obs}}
\mid Y
\right)
=
0.332.
$$

Thus, the grid transformation primarily resolves the apparent discrepancy in
the threshold-based disagreement statistic rather than the already small
difference in mean absolute disagreement.

The broader disagreement pattern is summarized in @fig-v1-disagreement-ppc.
The observed mean, median, 90th percentile, maximum and proportion of
disagreements of at least three score points are all compatible with their
posterior predictive distributions. The clearest departure is the frequency
of disagreements of at least two score points, which is higher in the observed
data than in most continuous replicated datasets. As shown above, this
discrepancy is substantially reduced once replicated grades are placed on the
same integer-valued 1--5 scale as the observations.

![Posterior predictive checks for several summaries of reviewer disagreement under V1. Histograms show statistics from replicated datasets and dashed vertical lines show the corresponding observed values.](figures/validation/v1_disagreement_ppc.png){#fig-v1-disagreement-ppc width=95% fig-pos="H"}
